Read this scene from a novel and say what it tells us about time. Don't work out a day number: only what the text says.

## End of the Previous Scene

To Come?" said Scrooge. The Spirit answered not, but pointed onward with its hand. "You are about to show me shadows of the things that have not happened, but will happen in the time before us," Scrooge pursued. "Is that so, Spirit?" The upper portion of the garment was contracted for an instant in its folds, as if the Spirit had inclined its head. That was the only answer he received. Although well used to ghostly company by this time, Scrooge feared the silent shape so much that his legs trembled beneath him, and he found that he could hardly stand when he prepared to follow it. The Spirit paused a moment, as observing his condition, and giving him time to recover. But Scrooge was all the worse for this. It thrilled him with a vague uncertain horror, to know that behind the dusky shroud, there were ghostly eyes intently fixed upon him, while he, though he stretched his own to the utmost, could see nothing but a spectral hand and one great heap of black. "Ghost of the Future!" he exclaimed, "I fear you more than any spectre I have seen. But as I know your purpose is to do me good, and as I hope to live to be another man from what I was, I am prepared to bear you company, and do it with a thankful heart. Will you not speak to me?" It gave him no reply. The hand was pointed straight before them. "Lead on!" said Scrooge. "Lead on! The night is waning fast, and it is precious time to me, I know. Lead on, Spirit!" The Phantom moved away as it had come towards him. Scrooge followed in the shadow of its dress, which bore him up, he thought, and carried him along.

## Scene: merchants-discuss-dead-man

They scarcely seemed to enter the city; for the city rather seemed to spring up about them, and encompass them of its own act. But there they were, in the heart of it; on 'Change, amongst the merchants; who hurried up and down, and chinked the money in their pockets, and conversed in groups, and looked at their watches, and trifled thoughtfully with their great gold seals; and so forth, as Scrooge had seen them often.

The Spirit stopped beside one little knot of business men. Observing that the hand was pointed to them, Scrooge advanced to listen to their talk.

"No," said a great fat man with a monstrous chin, "I don't know much about it, either way. I only know he's dead."

"When did he die?" inquired another.

"Last night, I believe."

"Why, what was the matter with him?" asked a third, taking a vast quantity of snuff out of a very large snuff-box. "I thought he'd never die."

"God knows," said the first, with a yawn.

"What has he done with his money?" asked a red-faced gentleman with a pendulous excrescence on the end of his nose, that shook like the gills of a turkey-cock.

"I haven't heard," said the man with the large chin, yawning again. "Left it to his company, perhaps. He hasn't left it to me. That's all I know."

This pleasantry was received with a general laugh.

"It's likely to be a very cheap funeral," said the same speaker; "for upon my life I don't know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?"

"I don't mind going if a lunch is provided," observed the gentleman with the excrescence on his nose. "But I must be fed, if I make one."

Another laugh.

"Well, I am the most disinterested among you, after all," said the first speaker, "for I never wear black gloves, and I never eat lunch. But I'll offer to go, if anybody else will. When I come to think of it, I'm not at all sure that I wasn't his most particular friend; for we used to stop and speak whenever we met. Bye, bye!"

Speakers and listeners strolled away, and mixed with other groups. Scrooge knew the men, and looked towards the Spirit for an explanation.



## Instructions

Output each field on its own labeled line.

TIME_RELATION: [when this scene happens relative to the scene before it in reading order — one of: continues (picks up at the same time or moments later), later (some time after it), earlier (before it: a flashback or a recollection told as a scene, including a past that a spirit, dream or vision shows a character; also a scene whose present is only a line or a short lead-in before it mostly tells the past, such as a story a character tells or the narrator's account of someone's youth, but not one where the present has real action on the page around the telling), frame (narration from after the story, looking back), vision (events that have not happened, or may not happen, as the story tells them: a prophecy, a future a character is shown that may be averted, a dream of what might come; the past is always earlier, even when a spirit, a dream or a vision shows it), unclear]
TIME_GAP: [the gap from the previous scene in at most six words, no explanation: "an hour", "the next morning", "three weeks", "five years", "several weeks"; empty if none is stated or implied]
TIME_ANCHOR: [a calendar fact pinning when THIS scene's action happens — a date, weekday, month, season, holiday or named day ("the hottest day of the summer") — quoted briefly; not a habit ("every Friday") or a date the scene only mentions; empty if none]
TIME_REFERS: [any statement in this scene of how long ago or how long until another event in the story, quoted briefly: "that June night three months before", "five years since he'd seen her", "the funeral was on the third day"; separate several with semicolons; empty if none]
TIME_SPAN: [when the scene summarizes a stretch of time ("all that summer"), how long; empty for a scene that plays out in one sitting]
TIME_DATE: [only what this scene's own text states about the calendar date, in EDTF: "1922-07-04", "XXXX-07-04" when the year isn't given here, "1922" for a year, "1922-22" for summer 1922 (21 spring, 22 summer, 23 autumn, 24 winter), "1917~" for "around 1917", "1922-06/1922-09" for a stretch. A date the text fixes by a stated distance from a named calendar day counts as given, marked ~: "In two weeks it'll be the longest day in the year" → "XXXX-06-07~". Never fill in a part the text doesn't give; empty if the text gives no date]
